items.question: What was it about Microsoft's Photosynth demo that drew you into computer vision?
items.object: Microsoft's Photosynth demo
items.answer: I saw this demo from Microsoft in 2008 or so. It's called Photosynth. I actually saw this in a TED Talk. And if you took pictures on a vacation and then gave it to Photosynth, it would stitch all those pictures in 3D, like basically it multi-view registration and stuff. Well, I didn't know all of the terms then, but it was just magical to me that it would match one picture with another. And I was thinking about it as like, "How do they compare pixel by pixel?" as a naive programmer. So I started getting really into it.

items.question: How did you understand the central difference between your 2012 ConvNet paper and the handcrafted-feature methods that dominated computer vision at the time?
items.object: End-to-end ConvNet learning versus handcrafted-feature methods in computer vision
items.answer: Back then, the landscape of computer vision / machine learning was you used features. You used SIFT, hog features, a bunch of these handcrafted features that people spent years refining, and then you extracted those features, and then you sent them into an SVM, like a kernel SVM of some sort. And that was the state of the art, and mostly what people were adjusting and tweaking was the features themselves. Like, are you using SIFT? What parameters? Are you using SIFT and hog? What about these other things? What about SURF and various other things? And the other thing you tweaked was the classifier itself, which was like, which SVM are you using? Or are you using an SVM? Are you using an RBF kernel? Are you using kernel for the SVM? Just to project it up. So primarily exploration was in those knobs. And our paper did ConvNets, which was completely the thesis: you don't need to do any of those things. Just do end-to-end learning. Just take pixels and then push it through a neural network, and then you mostly modify the loss, the model architecture, and the pre-processing of the images.

items.question: How do you view the computer vision community’s response to Alex Krizhevsky’s 2012 ImageNet results?
items.object: The computer vision community's adoption of neural networks after Alex Krizhevsky's ImageNet results
items.answer: It all changed in December 2012 after Alex Krizhevsky published his ImageNet results. People basically within two years—I mean, there was obviously that phase of like you don't believe it, you downplay it, you're like, "Oh, this is just a fad or whatever." But there was that healthy phase in the scientific community of not believing and being extremely skeptical, and then started accepting it. And actually, one of my friends was a grad student at that time, the guy who wrote Caffe. He had to tiptoe around his advisor to work on Caffe and work on neural networks because his advisor was not supportive of working on these methods at all. So I think there's that large shift, especially in the younger people who were like, "This is the future. I don't know what these professors are thinking." And within two years, everyone changed their mind. There wasn't really much pushback, but yeah. And now, today, it's all neural networks.

items.question: How do you understand established researchers’ reluctance to embrace new scientific methods?
items.object: Established researchers’ skepticism toward new scientific methods
items.answer: I think there are a couple of things. One is a sunk cost fallacy, right? So if you basically invested 10 years of your life into a certain expertise, you would want to give that a fair shot before you give up on it. The other thing is there are genuinely fads that come and go and they last for longer than you think, and the older, more experienced people do see some of these fads come and go and they want to make sure this new thing isn't really a fad. So I think it's completely fair for people to have that position, but also have other people completely counter that position and prove them wrong.

items.question: Why did you decide to stop working on GANs despite their popularity?
items.object: GANs and the decision to stop researching them
items.answer: GANs came and went. You know, if you talk to someone in 2017, they would look at you like a fool if you said GANs were a passing fad because half the papers were being written about GANs, right? I stopped working on GANs at some point because I just thought they were so unstable and it was not clear that they could be stabilized. I developed this conviction over a couple of years, but also François Chollet wrote this beautiful blog post around how GANs are unstable and we need to take a very close look on how to stabilize them before making them realistically mainstream. And I was like, I'm not a theoretical mathematician. It's not my expertise. I also fully agree that GANs are highly unstable and it's not clear how they work, what the dynamics are. So I shelved my work on GANs purely because I was like, "I'll just wait for a few years until someone figures this out because it's not in my interest to work on this." But that's an example of a fad.

items.question: How do you approach choosing research problems and methods?
items.object: Choosing research problems and methods
items.answer: I don't really focus on some kind of principled search of some grand problem or whatever. In some sense, I'm a very empirical scientist. I ask questions that are very grounded in reality and that look fairly like an applied question, except to actually get there you probably need to solve a bunch of fundamental problems. So, I guess to actually characterize it in a slightly different way: there are scientists who are clear about answering questions, and there are scientists who care about understanding methods. There are various kinds of scientists. Some of them are married to the method or the technology. Some of them are married to the outcome, the end result. I'm very much of the latter. So I generally just explore whatever seems cool in turn and promising in terms of methods.

items.question: How did your experience researching GANs lead you to move on from them?
items.object: Moving on from GAN research
items.answer: Wasserstein GAN was me and my really close friend Martin Arjovsky. Martin was my intern the previous summer and we worked together in StarCraft. We would chat about a million different things, and Martin is a proper mathematician. He had this cool theory that Wasserstein distances in GANs are related and stuff, and so I helped him out on making that into a concrete work. Like, sure, you have your starting point, but here's how we prove it out. Here's how we actually do experiment design. And then I actually think I helped run a bunch of experiments and actually wrote most of the code. So yeah, that's my journey with GANs. After Wasserstein GANs and through that journey I was generally frustrated by how it felt like we were just searching for a needle in a haystack rather than doing something a bit more principled. After I was frustrated with GANs, there's two things that happened. One, I got frustrated with GANs anyways, and the other, PyTorch also published right at that time, and I just got really busy with PyTorch. Already being frustrated with GANs, I just was like, "You know what? That's it."

items.question: How would you characterize the ML framework landscape when you started doing research?
items.object: The ML framework landscape when Soumith Chintala began doing research
items.answer: When I started, ML frameworks—there were no binary installs. You had to install from source. And the documentation was pretty sketchy. And they were written in all kinds of languages. When I was getting started, I used an ML framework written in C++. The next year, I used one written in Lua. For my homeworks, I used one written in Lisp. And a bunch of people at that time were using Theano, which was written in Python. So it was a healthy mix of things. And these were tiny projects, mostly developed by a couple of grad students in their free time. And the year after I graduated from my master's, Caffe started being popular. It's also written in C++. And by the time I started working at FAIR, I think there were like 15. There were 15 machine learning frameworks that were an active battlefield of frameworks that were trying to differentiate themselves with X or Y or Z.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between competition among machine learning frameworks around 2014 and the consolidated framework ecosystem today?
items.object: Low-level competition among machine learning frameworks around 2014
items.answer: Differentiating themselves with the same stuff, right? Ease of use, performance, flexibility, accessibility, the size of your ecosystem, examples, documentation. The concept of a model zoo just started getting introduced, started by Caffe. That was another differentiating factor, which is, "Hey, do you have pre-trained weights for something state of the art?" And I want to explain the level of detail here: in 2014 people had their own secretive convolution kernels that they didn't release because they were the secret sauce that made their research better or whatever. So there were labs, for example at NYU, where this guy Sixian Zhang wrote these fast convolution kernels that NYU kept for themselves as, "This is a secret of our lab and we wrote our research with this." So there was a healthy amount of that. The point I'm trying to make is the granularity of details here is not the same as what you think of today when you think of machine learning frameworks. People really did a bunch of things at a very low level and had to keep themselves competitive. This company Nirvana, which eventually got sold to Intel, had this guy Scott Gray who's now at OpenAI who was legendary at writing fast GEMM and convolution kernels that were faster than anything Nvidia had ever written. I mean, this goes back at least eight years at this point, but I believe Nirvana actually raised a bunch of money purely because Scott Gray wrote those kernels. So it was significant IP. Machine learning frameworks were significantly more low level. The actual differential between these frameworks and the intellectual property that was considered valuable was fairly low level, and a lot of people were very comfortable with doing that. That is now very consolidated. You just do PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow. You don't really know or care or understand what's going on at the deeper levels, and you just assume someone somewhere has consolidated and is doing the best job out there.

items.question: Why do you see FlashAttention and the bitsandbytes library as distinctive contributions to machine learning frameworks?
items.object: FlashAttention and the bitsandbytes library as contributions to machine learning frameworks
items.answer: I think in the most recent times, the only work I've seen in probably the last three or four years that tried to add fundamental value that complements machine learning frameworks are either from Tri Dao and team, who did the whole FlashAttention work, or from Tim Dettmers, who does the bitsandbytes library. So I think those are the only two distinctive ones I remember where, from the systems side, deeply into the framework, you're injecting substantial value that isn't just given out of the box out of the framework.

items.question: What made Torch appealing to you compared with the EB Learn machine learning framework you had been using at NYU?
items.object: Torch's ease of use compared with EB Learn
items.answer: When I came to NYU, I was working on this machine learning framework called EB Learn. It was 2010, 2011. This was in C++, heavily templated C++. It would take 15 minutes to compile. It was just weird. And then I saw Torch the next year because one of the authors, Clément Farabet, was visiting the lab at NYU. And it just felt so much easier to use. It was a scripting thing. It didn't have any compile time. It was so easy and fast to iterate upon. That's how I got into using it.

items.question: How did you understand your responsibility when you became a maintainer of Torch?
items.object: The responsibilities of maintaining Torch
items.answer: I wrote them an email at some point saying, "Hey, you're taking so long to merge PRs. I'm sending all these fixes. Can you please do better? This is not okay." And so they actually replied saying, "Hey, why don't you become a maintainer? Just take over." So that's how I started maintaining Torch. And once you become a maintainer, it's kind of a responsibility. You're really focusing on growing the ecosystem as well. So it's not just the code stuff. It's everything. Go evangelize it, give talks, all of that stuff, right?

items.question: How do you think helping users shaped your product vision for machine learning platforms?
items.object: Developing product vision for machine learning platforms
items.answer: I think this wasn't some kind of prolific vision that I woke up one day and I was like, "Oh, this is what we need to build." But I think it is pretty safe to say at this stage that I have a reasonably good product vision, especially in ML platforms. And I think a lot of my getting good at this was because I was deeply helping out people with their problems and I put myself in their shoes routinely. So I think the 10,000 plus hours that I spent helping people, all the way from answering questions to spending hours and hours sitting and helping them debug stuff or, if they ask me how something can be done better, spending my own time trying to deeply think and understand how it can be done better, that really shaped how I think about these things.

items.question: What does usability in software tools mean to you?
items.object: Usability in software tools
items.answer: A lot of it obviously boils down to usability, and usability is hard to measure, but it basically drills down to the feeling that you get when you feel an adrenaline boost when you get something done on the computer using something. You just did it and it's like, "Oh yeah, it's working. That's amazing." The fastest time to get there, in my opinion, is usability. This can be something from a micro decision, like saving two clicks to do something that you do every day, all the way to being able to think clearly. If you have an idea, there's a bunch of tools you use to actually make that idea a reality. If the tools are more usable, you can execute that idea into reality much more clearly. I wouldn't say much more quickly; that depends. But you can just keep that idea as a center point of your head instead of putting that idea through multiple convoluted things that make you lose track of what you're trying to do in the first place. So usability really, I think, is a very subjective thing that drills down multiple ways, but getting out of the way, being efficient, there's all these things. So I think I've developed a sense of that eventually helping me build PyTorch.

items.question: Why did you build a strong user feedback cycle into PyTorch from the beginning?
items.object: Iterative product development and early PyTorch user feedback
items.answer: I was pretty convinced by that time that you can never get a framework or product right in the first iteration. It doesn't matter how much of a genius you are. In the first iteration, you only directionally get to where you should be. So when we built PyTorch, we had a strong feedback cycle that we explicitly set up from the get-go, where every week we would onboard a few of our friends and eventually a few of our friends' friends to use it, and then we would just be available. We would be like, "All right, if you see any problem, just ping us. You can even call us on our cell or something." So that iteration, I think by the time we actually released PyTorch to the world, we had about 100 iterations of PyTorch already. That significantly changes things. This is not just for PyTorch; if I build any product, that's just how I would do it again.

items.question: How did you decide which kinds of AI innovation PyTorch should prioritize?
items.object: PyTorch's decision to prioritize modelers and architectural innovation
items.answer: I think it's pretty important to be explicit about what are the knobs people care about in your product. At some point I wrote down, "Okay, what are the types of innovation that are happening in AI?" There's basically better neural network structures, better optimization methods, scaling to larger neural networks, defining more clever objective functions, injecting better priors into pre-processing and post-processing, collecting better data labels, clever labels, various training regimes that are different, like instead of supervised you do unsupervised games or semi-supervised things, using hardware more efficiently, speed of training, speed of deployment, latency, that kind of stuff. These are all the knobs people use to make progress. So then when we're building the framework, I looked very explicitly at what are the knobs that we should be betting on. Obviously making a framework that allows you to tune all these knobs all at the same time in a very efficient way is not possible or easy, and that is just one of those paradox of choice kind of things. You need to pick and choose what you're going to enable your users more than others. So we picked this thesis that modeling innovation, that is architectural innovations, are going to continue to be one of the most important things in making, pushing the field forward for the next few years. So we just said, "Okay, that's what we're going for." So then you have to keep the modeler at the center of your universe. There's a modeler, there's the back-end engineer, there's a few personas, right? If you build a framework that is absolutely optimized for the modeler to be flexible and do their work most productively, it will come at a cost with making back-end engineers happier. That was our thesis. And so we were very explicit when we built the first sketches. Just having that clear thesis of what you're betting on, if the product has to be successful, you don't just try to do everything. You bet on some things and you're hoping that your bet is true and that amplifies the structural advantage to your product.

These are all the knobs people use to make progress. So then when we're building the framework, I looked very explicitly at what are the knobs that we should be betting on. Obviously making a framework that allows you to tune all these knobs all at the same time in a very efficient way is not possible or easy, and that is just one of those paradox of choice kind of things. You need to pick and choose what you're going to enable your users more than others. So we picked this thesis that modeling innovation, that is architectural innovations, are going to continue to be one of the most important things in making, pushing the field forward for the next few years. items.question: How did you think about designing PyTorch's user support channels?
items.object: The design of PyTorch's user support and community channels
items.answer: As part of the first thing around feedback and users, apart from the initial product iteration thing, I had enough experience over the six years before in supporting users, answering their questions, and understanding how at a larger scale feedback cycles tend to be. So we very carefully designed within PyTorch how people would, if they faced a problem, what would happen. We explicitly designed forums, which could be Google indexable—not Google Group Forums, which are crappy, but we used this new thing. And then we had a very high-touch, low-volume thing called a PyTorch Slack, and we would only invite people who crossed a certain level of competence in PyTorch because we knew supporting via chat was very expensive and draining for everyone involved. So we didn't want people to come in and put a giant message and say, "I got this error. Can someone help me?" because that was way better suited for the forums than Slack. Slack would be way more productive if we had more meaningful discussions. And then we had the Twitter account where we set up a bunch of monitors if anyone anywhere mentioned PyTorch on the internet, we would get a message and we would amplify the high-quality projects. So that stuff goes into the first bucket I talked about, which we were really explicit about.

items.question: How do you use Huffman coding as a way to think about PyTorch's API design?
items.object: PyTorch API design and Huffman coding
items.answer: The way I think about it is like Huffman coding, which is just how the most frequent things you write have to be written with the least amount of bits. It just makes it convenient, short, happy. So in PyTorch, in the API, it's not just the API options that are default are the best options, but also literally the most frequent functions are shorter in terms of the string length, just because we know that's pretty important.

items.question: How do you view François Chollet's principle of progressively exposing complexity in a deep learning framework?
items.object: François Chollet's principles of progressive disclosure of complexity
items.answer: François's principles, I read them, they're great. We're on the same page there. We think a lot about having really good defaults and exposing complexity in a way that is incremental, hierarchical. The way we think about it is most people in most scenarios shouldn't care about anything more than the defaults, and then those who care about it should get the absolute power to tweak it to death. I think we're on the same page there.

items.question: How do you approach community design for open-source software?
items.object: Community design for open-source software
items.answer: More broadly, I think it's hard to really generalize. Very broadly, Stack Overflow, that's one thing. There's a bunch of things that are good. Discourse is the forum we use, and Discourse themselves as a product really think about how community dynamics, engagement dynamics work and how to build the best software to promote certain dynamics and not promote certain dynamics and stuff. I think at a broad level, those are the kinds of things that people are working on, and that is awesome, and we're basically sitting on some of these efforts. I don't have a lot of thoughts or advice at a broad level because I think where I do focus on and probably excel at is not at the broad scale. Maybe it's not in my interest at the broad scale, but more of, let's think very carefully at the smaller scale and design this stuff.

items.question: How do you understand the differences between PyTorch and TensorFlow within the machine learning framework ecosystem?
items.object: PyTorch and TensorFlow
items.answer:
So at this point, PyTorch and TensorFlow have become large enough that they try to serve everyone. I think at this point the products are fairly similar, and I don't see a big difference as such. In isolation of just looking at the products, I don't think there's a lot of difference, especially if you look at it at a very high level where you're writing a slide about, "This product has this feature. This product has this other feature." You basically come with the same matrix of things. Both of them have the same features.

I think if you look at it either more granularly or more holistically, taking other aspects of a product that are not just the code and features, such as the ecosystem, such as how these products are designed from a usability perspective—usability never comes up in your feature checklist, right? Feature checklists are measurable, like, "It has quantization or stuff like that." In these aspects, I think there's a clear clustering of TensorFlow really designed for production from the beginning. While the features of both PyTorch and TensorFlow are at parity, the ecosystems do give a fairly different story.

PyTorch is dominantly used in research. The effects of that are if you're a researcher, you're probably using PyTorch because all of the stuff that I want to implement as baselines is just available in PyTorch. You wouldn't be using TensorFlow because it's that much harder to build out a bunch of things structurally. And I know this as someone who supported Torch, which is written in Lua, and Lua was a language that was written for microwaves and video games, right? So even something as basic as plotting would be a struggle in Lua, whereas Python had such fantastic packages. So I think in terms of ecosystems, TensorFlow structurally is not in a good place for research.

And I think the very interesting thing about production is production, in my opinion, doesn't have ecosystem effects in the same way research does. We've learned this over the years, where every employee at some company doing production is thinking about their company and their stack in a very specialized way. They're not like, "There's this serving platform for production. I'm going to use it." TorchServe or TensorFlow Serving and stuff don't get used in production in a way that you would expect people in research to reuse artifacts of the ecosystem. I think on the production side computationally, TensorFlow is obviously dominant because that's how they started as the production framework for Google. I think structurally, there isn't a big case to be made from an ecosystem effect.

There's a third category of people, data scientists and people who just use PyTorch or TensorFlow like they use scikit-learn. They just use the methods, they don't care about the subtleties, they use only a few knobs. I think there TensorFlow has dominated over the years and there's a significant ecosystem effect where TensorFlow offered various trainings and certification and things like that, and people were just trained in those things. So there's a whole layer of people in the data science space who at some point got TensorFlow certified or their company was using TensorFlow. So there ecosystem effects apply and TensorFlow, in my opinion, does dominate.

So there's these three buckets. I would say for researchers PyTorch dominates; for data scientists and stuff TensorFlow still dominates; and for production I think it's starting to get very hazy, where we see stuff in both ways. But if you think about the core product, we obviously still have DNA in the product experience itself, but from a feature checklist, I don't think there's a difference.

items.question: Why do you consider explicit tensor aliasing and view semantics important in a framework like PyTorch?
items.object: Tensor aliasing and view semantics in machine learning frameworks
items.answer: The very concept of an N-dimensional array as a programmable object with methods and stuff has a long history. I wouldn't say Yann LeCun pioneered it. Mathematica, MATLAB, and all these did it. There's certain concepts of it that Yann LeCun and Léon Bottou did pioneer that you actually don't see in any other scientific frameworks. The concept of tensor aliasing/views is actually something that Yann and Léon pioneered through their work on Lush and the work before. That's thinking of your ND array as something very close to your logical memory on your system and manipulating it in that way rather than thinking of it as some array that is somehow stored. The semantics of these are pretty important. We tried before building PyTorch to build an attempt of PyTorch in Julia. Julia didn't have concrete aliasing semantics, which means that you never knew whether you got a copy of your tensor or a view of your tensor, which means if you tried to modify the copy, you don't know if the original thing got affected or not. And that was pretty naturally okay for both MATLAB users and Julia users. That's just a normative thing. Two problems arise here. One is when you do gradients, when you actually do the backprop, you do have to carefully think about these things. The other thing is when you care about memory being a precious resource, which it has been on GPUs, then you also have to care about things very carefully. So they definitely pioneered that stuff very early on.

items.question: How do you assess Yann LeCun and Léon Bottou's technical legacy in machine learning frameworks beyond tensor views?
items.object: Yann LeCun and Léon Bottou's contributions to machine learning framework design beyond tensor views
items.answer: There's a bunch of stuff that they pioneered for the machine learning community, but also was invented very parallelly in other communities, such as their framework could export their entire model into a C++ code generated module that you could just deploy without any dependency on Lisp. I think that was also simultaneously invented by MATLAB, MathWorks, with Simulink, the whole MATLAB Simulink stuff. They pioneered a bunch of automatic differentiation infrastructure in a way that is mainstream today. It's basically a function pointer to what produced it and stuff like that. Because automatic differentiation had so many manifestations, tape-based and so on, it also had so many granularities of manifestations. Even today if you look at automatic differentiation, there's a bunch of systems that are differentiating C programs. Literally, it's scalar differentiation that it reasons about from the get-go, or differentiates assembly. They, Yann and Léon, concretely only differentiated tensor types and reasoned about those and stuff. And then they did a bunch of stuff around Hessian tricks. The whole diagonal of the Hessian approximation to do second-order methods, they absolutely pioneered that stuff and implemented it. It was in their landmark 1999 paper as a small section, as if it's casually there. And that ended up becoming parts of Torch and Theano and a bunch of other things, pretty much re-implementing their approximations exactly as is.

items.question: How did your commitment to modelers shape the way you brought compilation to eager-mode PyTorch in version 2.0?
items.object: PyTorch 2.0’s approach to compiling eager-mode programs
items.answer: We bet on modelers and modeling being pretty important. One of the central effects of that thesis is eager mode, which, by the way, the term was invented by the TensorFlow people. We used to call it imperative mode. So basically what it means is when you're doing modeling, you iterate on your program without any other constraints. That is, you can write whatever code you want and that code is your model. And you shouldn't really be like, "I can't write this code because that's not allowed by my framework." So that's the whole thesis. You can write for loops, ifs, whiles, anything you want, and that's our problem. With PyTorch 2.0, one of the central things we absolutely want to nail was to keep that alive: it's our problem how to compile the program, and if we can't compile it or part of it, we shouldn't. You shouldn't be thinking or caring about it. You shouldn't be like, "I can't write this because then it won't get compiled or something." So we basically built 2.0 entirely around partial graphs. This is something that no one in the machine learning frameworks does. We're like, "We'll just trace the program and the parts that we can compile, we will, and the parts that we can't compile, we will just leave alone." That is what compiler writers actually hate. That's the trade-off. We explicitly were like, "Yeah, it's going to be harder to write the compiler, but we're not optimizing for the compiler people to have an easy life. We're optimizing for the modelers to have an easy life." So that's the central way to explain 2.0: you write your programs as is and it's not your problem whether stuff gets compiled or not, it's our problem, and we're going to do this without you noticing.

items.question: How do you think about building a robot that would actually be useful in your household?
items.object: Practical household robotics
items.answer: It all stems from I just hate to do household chores, basic stuff. Like just putting dishes in the dishwasher, taking them out, doing the laundry, not even folding clothes or anything. Literally just remembering to take clothes, put them in the laundry, turn it on, switch them to the dryer, turn it on. And I used to do robotics 13 years ago and I stopped because doing physical robots is just hard and annoying and rate limiting. It's just way less productive by design. And I started this again just because I was like, I don't know. I just feel more hopeful and passionate, and I feel like AI has made substantial progress that it feels like a good time to get into robotics. I have a few grounded rules. It has to be within a profile that supports being in a household. It has to be roughly a human profile or less. It has to be able to have a basic payload. It shouldn't be like, "Oh, I lifted 200 g and that's it." It has to be able to lift a plateful of food or various things like that. It has to be cheap. You know, I just don't work on things that are like, "Oh, this is going to be half a million dollars." And that's basically useful for nobody, including me. So I think at this stage in AI, we built a bunch of machine learning methods that work without having to have precise robots. I think the cheap part really can be drilled on by making robots that are not very good, but you can fix in software. You can basically say, "Oh, the ML model will deal with it." And then the basic goal is being able to treat the robot like it's a 4-year-old child. You think of a 4-year-old child and you say, "Hey, I will tell you detailed instructions on how to go get me a glass of water from the kitchen," and they're able to do it. They will break the sound into multiple steps and they would ask you some follow-up questions on the way like, "Where are the glasses again?" or something. And then you say, "Oh, hold it with two hands and be careful," all of that stuff. So the premise is to be able to treat the robot like it's imperfect in its motor skills, its language skills, and its visual perception and still make it useful in the household.

items.question: How close do you think household robotics is to being ready for a company to productize and ship?
items.object: Commercial readiness of household robotics
items.answer: I don't think it's anywhere close to the field itself being anywhere close to having any of this become a company and productionize it and ship it. I think that's at least 5 to 7 years away. We just have to de-risk it a lot more from a research angle. items.question: How do you think someone who wants to become an ML practitioner should develop their skills?
items.object: Developing a career as an ML practitioner
items.answer: I think people kind of—I would put them broadly in two buckets. One is people really want to have a career in ML, as in this one will be known as the ML person. For them, it is pretty obvious that they just have to get really good at first using all the tools in ML. And I don't mean software tools; I mean all tools, including software tools, various methods, getting good at understanding how to train networks. The software is not going to teach you about a bunch of other aspects, right? So just getting a good grasp of all the landscape, all the tools, all the methodologies, getting strong at executing, being principled, taking questions and being able to answer using ML. Just like a practitioner, I would call it. If you go ask a doctor, they're a practitioner of medical science, right? So similarly, they're just getting good at a bunch of the basics and the tooling and how to diagnose and things like that. It's similar for someone who wants to be the ML person. They see themselves as an ML practitioner and that's how they want to make their career. Just focus on doing as many hands-on projects as possible. That'll get you the experience in building out these tools, being able to get good at these tools.

items.question: What level of ML understanding do you think is enough for someone using it to pursue a different primary goal?
items.object: Learning ML as a tool for another primary pursuit
items.answer: There is the other kind of people who I would say are passersby. They basically think ML has huge potential and they want to use it, but it's not their primary focus. They're applying ML to do some other large thing. I guess some other thing. For them, in my opinion, it's mainly do a few projects really applying ML just so that you get a mental model of what ML can and cannot do as of today. And that's really good enough. As long as you get that kind of mental model, it becomes one of the several tools in your Rolodex and you know when to take it out and apply it.
